choices: The high-voltage backbone: balancing, frequency and system security
questions.explanation: The TSO runs transmission, keeps supply and demand balanced at 50 Hz, and maintains security; the DSO handles local distribution.

questions.prompt: Power is transmitted at **high voltage** mainly to…
choices: Reduce current and therefore resistive losses over distance
questions.explanation: Higher voltage means lower current for the same power, cutting I²R losses over long distances.

questions.prompt: If demand exceeds generation on the grid, the frequency…
questions.explanation: A supply shortfall slows the synchronous machines, dropping frequency; reserves are activated to restore it.

choices: Paying one plant down and another up to relieve congestion
Restarting the grid after a blackout
questions.explanation: When the market dispatch would overload a line, the TSO redispatches generation across the constraint to keep flows within limits.

questions.prompt: The **N-1 security criterion** means the grid must…
choices: Withstand the loss of any single element without cascading
Run one line at a time
questions.explanation: N-1 is the standard that the system survives any single failure — the basis for spare transmission and generation margin.

questions.prompt: Under **zonal** pricing (as in Europe), internal congestion is…
choices: Handled outside the market via redispatch
questions.explanation: Zonal markets set one price per zone and resolve internal congestion operationally through redispatch; nodal markets price it at each node.

questions.prompt: A region keeps building cheap wind but can't deliver it to cities. The most likely issue is…
choices: Too little demand response on the wind farm
questions.explanation: Generation outrunning the wires shows up as congestion, rising redispatch cost and connection queues — the grid is the bottleneck.

questions.prompt: The **grid-and-compute** thesis argues that data centres should be…
choices: Sited where grid/renewable headroom exists and operated flexibly to help balance the system
Built only in city centres regardless of grid
Run at constant full load with no grid awareness
Banned from connecting to the grid
questions.explanation: Treating siteable, flexible compute as a grid resource lets it monetise spare/curtailed renewables and provide demand response instead of straining the grid.

questions.prompt: Why can a large data centre be an **asset** to the grid rather than just a burden?
choices: It is siteable and partly flexible, so it can absorb curtailed power and provide demand response
It never draws power at peak
questions.explanation: Flexible, well-sited compute can soak up otherwise-curtailed renewables and shift load — firming demand instead of forcing reinforcement.

questions.prompt: **Co-locating** a data centre with generation (behind-the-meter) primarily helps by…
choices: Cutting transmission need and connection delay
questions.explanation: Serving the load on-site avoids loading the transmission grid and sidesteps multi-year connection queues.

questions.prompt: A load with a **high load factor** (like a data centre) is notable because it…
choices: Uses grid and generation capacity efficiently (steady, around-the-clock demand)
Only runs a few hours a year
questions.explanation: A flat, steady load uses expensive capacity efficiently — attractive economically, but also a large, constant draw on the grid.

questions.prompt: Rising **redispatch costs** in a system are best read as a signal that…
choices: Generation has outrun the transmission grid (congestion)
Frequency control has been switched off
questions.explanation: Growing redispatch spend means the cheapest flows repeatedly overload lines — an argument for grid build-out, storage, or siting load near supply.

questions.prompt: The **load factor** of a system is…
questions.explanation: Average load divided by peak load — high means flat/efficient use of capacity, low means peaky.

questions.prompt: The energy drawn by a steady load over a period is…
questions.explanation: Energy = power × time; for a varying load use the average power over the period.

questions.prompt: A system has average load 600 MW and peak load 1000 MW. Find its load factor (decimal).
A data centre draws a steady 100 MW for 24 hours. Find the energy consumed, in MWh.
